article_title: Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options
citation: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. http://www.ccsso.org
title: Strengthen home language surveys by stating purposes, targeting construct-essential questions, setting decision rules, and validating forms
description: The paper proposes minimal guidance for states to strengthen the reliability, validity, and usefulness of home language surveys in moving toward a common EL definition. States should "Clearly state the purposes and intended uses of the HLS", evaluate questions as construct-essential, construct-associated, or construct-irrelevant, "Establish clear guidelines for administering the survey, and clear decision rules for interpreting and acting on the information", and conduct validation reviews examining over- and under-identification including hit rates based on false positives and false negatives.
requirements: Survey questions should reflect the stated purposes and uses of the HLS
Rigorous translation of survey questions into multiple languages and guidelines for oral administration where adult literacy is an issue
constraints: Resource constraints may limit the feasibility of multiple measures at this stage
target_learners: K-12 students entering school who are potentially English learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate initial identification of students needing specialized language and academic support services
examples: The paper lists example construct-essential questions such as which language the child most frequently speaks at home and which language(s) the child currently understands or speaks
key_sources: Linquanti, R., & Cook, H. G. (2013). Toward a "Common Definition of English Learner": Guidance for States and State Assessment Consortia in Defining and Addressing Policy and Technical Issues and Options. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565753

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Five-dimension framework for strengthening Home Language Survey design and use
description: The working session structured its discussion of HLS improvement around five dimensions: "A. Purposes and intended uses B. Key constructs (aligned to purposes and uses) C. HLS question formulation (aligned to constructs) D. Administrative procedures E. Decision rules." The framework orders design work so that purposes guide construct selection, constructs guide question wording, and procedures and decision rules govern administration and interpretation of responses. The paper uses it to organize the session's consensus recommendations for states and assessment consortia.
requirements: Purposes and intended uses must be defined first, since they guide identification of key constructs and thus more precise HLS questions
constraints: Time to explore the decision-rules dimension was limited, and the paper says further discussion and elaboration of this dimension would be beneficial
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of students entitled to specialized English language development services and English language proficiency screening
examples: The session produced consensus statements under each dimension, from the three HLS purposes to sample Tier 1-3 questions and decision-rule guidelines
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Three-tier relevance taxonomy of HLS constructs: essential, associated, and irrelevant
description: The paper organizes HLS constructs by degree of relevance to a student's current English abilities. Essential constructs are "student's current language(s); frequency of English language use by student; frequency of English language exposure provided by others." Associated constructs include languages spoken among adults in the home, linguistic history, and years in U.S. schooling. Country of origin is classed as irrelevant. Participants considered student language dominance outmoded, focusing instead on contexts of exposure to English across home, school/child care, and recreational settings.
requirements: Essential constructs should appear as Tier 1 questions on a tiered intake form and associated constructs as Tier 2, with the HLS clearly demarcated in any multi-purpose intake form
constraints: Parents' language use among themselves but not with the student may be misleading, and reported first language may be inaccurate due to cultural pride
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners
target_learning_goals: Gauging the language environments a student has been exposed to and the likelihood the student has acquired English abilities before enrolling
examples: Tier 1 sample questions ask which languages the child currently understands, speaks, most often uses, and most often hears across home, school, and outside-of-school settings
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076
title: Three-level hierarchical linear modeling for meta-analyzing single-case experimental design data
description: The article uses a three-level hierarchical linear model in which DTT implementation fidelity observations (Level 1) are nested within participants (Level 2) within studies (Level 3). Phase is dummy-coded, time is centered on the last training session, and a moderator term tests BST or individual components. The authors state "HLM is able to analyze clustered data, or observations within participants and participants within studies", allowing effect sizes to vary across participants and studies while estimating one overall intervention effect. Lag 1 autocorrelation was modeled to control Type I error and improve power.
requirements: Raw single-case data retrievable in graphical or tabular form (via WebPlot Digitizer 2.0) so observations can be modeled at each level of nesting
constraints: HLM carries distributional assumptions, for example the assumption of homogeneous residuals, which the authors list as a potential limitation
Ignoring the natural hierarchy of data can lead to an underestimate of the standard error and an increase in Type I errors, per the authors
target_learners: Meta-analysts and researchers synthesizing single-case experimental design studies
target_learning_goals: Quantitative synthesis of intervention effects from clustered single-case data
examples: The model was fit in RStudio to 46 studies with 224 participants, with four models (BST, modeling, rehearsal, no moderator) and a Bonferroni correction of α = .05/4 = .0125.
key_sources: Joelle Fingerhut, & Mariola Moeyaert. (2022). Training Individuals to Implement Discrete Trials with Fidelity: A Meta-Analysis. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 37(4), 239–250. https://doi.org/10.1177/10883576221081076

article_title: Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies
citation: Pyle, K. K., & Fabiano, G. A. (2017). Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies. Manuscript submitted to Exceptional Children October 2016; accepted March 2017.
title: HLM-based meta-analysis of single-case design studies as a method for quantifying intervention evidence
description: The article develops and demonstrates a three-level hierarchical linear modeling approach to meta-analyzing single-subject design studies, where "Level 1 represents the data points, or repeated measures within persons", Level 2 represents students, and Level 3 represents studies. HLM was chosen because "HLM analyses can account for complex data structures (missing data, varying intervention lengths) likely to be found in single-case-design studies". The authors argue this method shows promise for addressing criticisms of statistical analysis of single-subject designs and supports continued inclusion of such designs in meta-analyses.
requirements: Graphed time-series data across baseline and intervention phases must be available for effect size calculation
Data points are coded for phase and reversal order, and outcomes converted to common percentage metrics
constraints: The authors note the number of studies and participants was small, which may limit generalizability of study-level moderator findings
target_learners: Students with ADHD (as demonstrated); method applies to single-case intervention research broadly
target_learning_goals: Quantifying behavioral intervention effects across single-case studies
examples: The Cottone (1998) dissertation was removed as an outlier due to floor effects in its disruptive-behavior goal, illustrating a data consideration for this method.
key_sources: Pyle, K. K., & Fabiano, G. A. (2017). Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies. Manuscript submitted to Exceptional Children October 2016; accepted March 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED583708

article_title: A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals' competencies related to health literacy.
citation: Mac Olivia, Marshall Sarah, McFadden Kathleen, Ayre Julie, McCaffery Kirsten J, Billah Sk Masum, Muscat Danielle M. (2026). A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals’ competencies related to health literacy. Health Promotion International. https://doi.org/10.1093/heapro/daaf227
title: Health Literacy Knowledge and Experience Survey (HLKES)
description: The Health Literacy Knowledge and Experience Survey (HLKES), developed by Cormier and Kotrlik (2009), was the most frequently used measure in the review, employed in 13 additional studies (14 studies in total). The review notes it was also modified into the shortened HLKES-2 and culturally adapted and translated in several studies. The authors caution that "frequency of use is not necessarily an indicator of quality" and that the HLKES focuses primarily on personal health literacy and patient deficits, such as identifying patients at risk of having low health literacy.
requirements: Used to assess health professionals’ health literacy knowledge and experiences
constraints: Published in 2006, prior to recent shifts in emphasis towards organizational health literacy and systems-level change; focuses primarily on personal health literacy and patient deficits
key_sources: Mac Olivia, Marshall Sarah, McFadden Kathleen, Ayre Julie, McCaffery Kirsten J, Billah Sk Masum, Muscat Danielle M. (2026). A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals’ competencies related to health literacy. Health Promotion International. https://doi.org/10.1093/heapro/daaf227

article_title: Development and psychometric validation of a health literacy competency scale for nurses, and its application in a cross-sectional survey: a methodological study.
citation: Bao Xuemei, Liu Shuhan, Hu Xiaoxiao, Zhang Qinghua, Jiang Mei, Gan Yingting and Wang Yu. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of a health literacy competency scale for nurses, and its application in a cross-sectional survey: a methodological study. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1978033
title: Health Literacy Competencies Scale for Nurses (HLC-N): a 39-item, five-dimension instrument
description: The HLC-N is a nurse-specific health literacy competency assessment tool developed via literature review, interviews, and a two-round Delphi process with 16 experts. "The final scale comprises 39 items across five dimensions: Health Literacy Knowledge (7 items), Health Education Communication Competency (8 items), Health Education Practice Competency (8 items), Inter-professional and Resource Collaboration Competency (10 items), and Attitude and Motivation (6 items)." It uses a 5-point Likert format with two reverse-scored items and a total score range of 39–195.
requirements: Requires respondents to be in-service registered nurses with at least one year of clinical experience
constraints: Developed and validated in the Chinese cultural context; authors note the need to validate across diverse nursing populations
key_sources: Bao Xuemei, Liu Shuhan, Hu Xiaoxiao, Zhang Qinghua, Jiang Mei, Gan Yingting and Wang Yu. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of a health literacy competency scale for nurses, and its application in a cross-sectional survey: a methodological study. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1978033

article_title: Validation of health literacy competencies for healthcare professionals in Korea: a psychometric evaluation study.
citation: Kang Soo Jin, Hwang Won Ju, Park Chanho, Han Hae-Ra. (2026). Validation of health literacy competencies for healthcare professionals in Korea: a psychometric evaluation study. BMC Medical Education 26:244. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08605-0
title: Health literacy competencies (HLCs) four-domain framework: knowledge, skills, attitudes, and practice
description: The HLCs framework, first established by Coleman and colleagues in the US, conceptualizes the health literacy competencies healthcare professionals need as four domains. The article states: "HLCs comprise four domains: knowledge, skills, attitudes, and practice." The instrument items cover knowledge of health literacy and risk factors, attitudes toward communicating with patients with limited literacy, communication skills such as plain language and teach-back, and practices in patient education. The study validated this structure empirically in Korea.
requirements: Items must be adapted to the healthcare context and professional roles of the applying country, as the Delphi process excluded items unsuitable for Korea
constraints: The framework was operationalized differently across countries; only one prior study reported psychometric properties before this one, per the article's background
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, attitudes, skills, and practices needed to communicate effectively with patients of varying health literacy
examples: The study retained the four-factor structure in the final 43-item Korean instrument without post-hoc model re-specification
key_sources: Kang Soo Jin, Hwang Won Ju, Park Chanho, Han Hae-Ra. (2026). Validation of health literacy competencies for healthcare professionals in Korea: a psychometric evaluation study. BMC Medical Education 26:244. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08605-0
